terms.definition: These are AI architectures designed to internalize the underlying laws of physics—such as gravity, friction, and conservation—rather than just predicting the next visual frame in a sequence. By representing the causal structure of an environment, these models allow embodied AI to accurately simulate the consequences of an action before executing it in the real world.
terms.analogy: A standard AI is like a photo of a kitchen that looks perfect but is made of cardboard; a Physically Viable World Model is a functioning kitchen where the AI knows that if it lets go of a glass, it will shatter on the floor due to gravity.
terms.business_value: This is the bridge between 'hallucinating' AI and reliable industrial automation. For leaders in logistics, manufacturing, or robotics, it reduces the risk of expensive hardware damage and allows for safer, faster deployment of autonomous systems in unpredictable environments.

terms.definition: This refers to the process where an LLM agent autonomously updates its external 'harness'—the specific prompts, tool instructions, and memory sets—based on its performance data. Unlike traditional fine-tuning which changes the model's core weights, self-evolution refines the operational framework surrounding the AI to improve task execution without expensive retraining.
terms.analogy: Think of the LLM as a car's engine; you aren't rebuilding the engine every day, but the car is autonomously adjusting its tire pressure, suspension, and GPS routing (the harness) based on the specific terrain it just drove over to ensure the next trip is smoother.
terms.business_value: It moves AI from a static tool to a self-improving asset. This significantly lowers the 'Total Cost of Ownership' for AI agents because the system handles its own maintenance and optimization, reducing the need for constant human prompt engineering and troubleshooting.

terms.definition: This is the ability of an AI system to intelligently select and utilize external software tools (APIs, databases, or calculators) across diverse and unfamiliar environments. It requires the model to maintain state across multiple steps and coordinate complex reasoning strategies to solve problems that a single model cannot handle alone.
terms.analogy: It is the difference between a kitchen appliance that can only toast bread and a Master Chef who can walk into any kitchen, identify the available tools—from a whisk to a sous-vide machine—and figure out how to use them in the right order to prepare a banquet.
terms.business_value: This solves the problem of 'tool brittleness.' For the enterprise, this means AI agents can finally be integrated into complex, multi-software workflows (like cross-departmental ERP and CRM tasks) without breaking every time the software interface or the specific task parameters change.
